scenes.text: Power in rotational dynamics. By the end, you will have derived one equation. Torque times angular velocity, built from nothing but work and time.
Begin with work. A force pushing an object through a distance does work. That single idea is all we need to start.
Power is how fast work happens. Work done, divided by the time it takes. Take force times distance, and divide by time. Distance over time is velocity.
So for straight line motion, power equals force times velocity. Keep that picture in mind. We are about to bend the straight line into a circle.
Now the body is pinned at a centre, and it turns. The force acts at some radius. Distance is replaced by angle, and we measure angle in radians.
Torque is force times the perpendicular distance from the axis. For a small turn, a point on the rim moves a small distance. Radius times the small angle.
So the small amount of work is force times radius, times the small angle. Force times radius is torque. So work equals torque times the angle turned.
Now divide by the small time. Work over time is power. Angle over time is angular velocity. And there it is. Power equals torque times angular velocity.
Check the units. Torque is newton metres. Angular velocity is radians per second. A radian is a pure number. So we are left with joules per second, the watt.
There is a second route. Rotational kinetic energy is one half times moment of inertia times angular velocity squared. Differentiate that in time. You get torque times angular velocity again.
A motor delivers forty newton metres of torque at one hundred radians per second. Multiply them. Four thousand watts. That is four kilowatts.
So, from absolute basics. Work is torque times angle. Power is work per unit time. Therefore, power equals torque times angular velocity.
